It is worth noting here that when the weight of atoms was discovered in the nineteenth century, Engels commented that Epicurus had already known that atoms had weight, although he had understood it in his own particular way.
For Democritus, the movement of atoms through the void came from mechanical necessity.
Epicurus introduced the weight of atoms into the theory. This opened a new way of looking at the problem.
He began to look to the weight of the atom itself for the source of its movement through empty space. In other words, he treated weight as an internal property of the atom.
That was the first result of Epicurus’s idea.
It had a second result as well.
Epicurus argued that the number of atoms was the only thing about them that was infinite.

The number of possible atomic shapes, by contrast, was finite. An atom’s shape depended on its weight, and its weight remained within certain limits. Its possible shapes were therefore limited as well.
More important, however, Epicurus’s introduction of weight allowed him to consider two closely connected questions at the same time: what causes atoms to move, and what path does that movement take?
As he developed the argument, he reached the following conclusion.
If atoms have weight, there is no reason to accept Democritus’s claim that they can move only in a straight line.
Instead, Epicurus argued that their spontaneous motion, arising internally from their own weight, can take the form of a swerve away from the straight line.
The angle of this swerve, he believed, was determined by the atom’s weight.
Epicurus made a rather simple assumption when he thought that this atomic swerve could help explain human freedom.
In this way he tried to escape the determinism of Democritus, who had completely denied that atoms could depart from a straight path.
But however simple Epicurus’s assumption may have been, his idea that atoms could swerve away from a straight line made a notable contribution to the development of ancient Greek materialism.
In it we can see an attempt to find the source of matter’s motion within matter itself.
This was understood as a challenge to the idea of a divine mover, or a divine source responsible for the motion of all things.
In short, Epicurus’s philosophy held that the world is material.
It denied the existence of immaterial spirits.
Everything in the world is made from eternal and indestructible atoms.
Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing ends in nothing.
So far, we have looked at atomism in its Greek forms, especially in the work of Leucippus, Democritus, and Epicurus.
This account shows that Greek atomism had a materialist direction in the way it understood the origin of the world, its motion, its development, and its fate.
In Indian sources, atomic ideas appeared in a different form.
We find some version of these ideas in a number of Indian philosophical schools. But atomism reached a more complete and distinctive form in one school in particular: the Nyaya–Vaisheshika school.

According to Deliprasad Chattopadhyaya and other historians of Indian philosophy, including Radhakrishnan—one of India’s most prominent philosophers and the author of History of Indian Philosophy—Nyaya–Vaisheshika had several features that set it apart from other Indian schools.
One of these was its special interest in atomism.
The school’s name combines the names of two earlier schools that merged in the third century BCE and became a single tradition.
One was the Nyaya school. The other was the Vaisheshika school.
Their doctrines were set out in two works, the Nyaya Sutra and the Vaisheshika Sutra.
The strong interest in atomism within this combined school was something new in Indian philosophy. From there, atomic ideas began to spread from one school to another.

Some historians date the emergence of this development within Nyaya–Vaisheshika to the second century BCE, around the same period in which atomism was taking a more developed form in Greek philosophy.
Because of this, many scholars of Indian philosophy argued that Indian thinkers had borrowed atomic theory from the Greeks.
Among them was the British scholar Keith, who presented this view in his book Indian Logic and Atomism, published by Oxford University Press in 1921.
But Chattopadhyaya, whom we mentioned above, tried to challenge this explanation.

“Quite apart from the possibility that philosophical ideas may develop independently and in parallel in different countries with similar social conditions—a possibility that this hypothesis clearly ignores altogether—there is another point to consider.
“For a foreign, ‘borrowed’ idea to take root in new soil, that soil must already be prepared to receive it.

“So even if we accept that Greek influence helped shape the ideas of Nyaya–Vaisheshika, we still have to study the social conditions in India—conditions which, in their general features, may have resembled those of Greece. Only those conditions could have made the acceptance and further development of these ideas possible.

“There is another point as well. Those who support the idea of complete and wholesale borrowing ignore the fact that the Nyaya Sutra and the Vaisheshika Sutra, although they remind us in some respects of Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle, contain a great deal more than we find in those thinkers.

“Moreover, those three ancient Greek philosophers did not, in the final analysis, represent the same philosophy that appears in Nyaya–Vaisheshika. Nor did they hold the same atomic theories, the same related ideas, the same judgments and conclusions, or the same philosophical categories. These things are not simply the same as they were in Greek philosophy. Here, in Nyaya–Vaisheshika, they appear as parts of a new Indian philosophy.”
8 — The Main Ideas of Ancient Indian Atomism
We therefore need to look at Indian atomism in its own right, rather than treating it in exactly the same way as Greek atomism.
Two questions need to be answered.
What were the main ideas in the atomic theories of Nyaya–Vaisheshika?
And how did this school understand essence?
Indian thinkers spoke of nine kinds of essence.
The first four, however, had a special place in their philosophy: earth, water, fire, and air.
Each of these four essences could be understood in two forms: an eternal form and a non-eternal form.
Chattopadhyaya explains the distinction as follows:
“By the eternal form of these essences they meant their atoms. By the non-eternal form they meant the combinations formed from those atoms.

“According to the Nyaya–Vaisheshika theory, atoms are not all alike in quality. Atoms of earth differ qualitatively from atoms of water and from the atoms of the other essences. The same is true of the atoms of water, fire, and air.”
Here we can see one difference between the atomism of Democritus and that of Nyaya–Vaisheshika.
But there was also another intellectual current in India, known as the Jaina tradition, which was interested in atomism.
Its interest was less intense than that of Nyaya–Vaisheshika, but the Jaina current had already taken shape several centuries before that school.
It also differed from Nyaya–Vaisheshika in an important respect: it accepted the idea that atoms were qualitatively alike.
So the disagreements over atomism did not exist only between Indian and Greek philosophy. They also existed among the different Indian atomic schools themselves.
In any case, the followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika tried to prove that atoms differed qualitatively.
They argued in roughly the following way:
Even the tiny particles that we can see only in a beam of sunlight entering a room through a small opening are not ultimate particles. They too are made up of smaller parts.
But this process of division cannot continue forever. There must be some point at which it ends.

Their reasoning was that if division were truly infinite, size itself would ultimately disappear as a meaningful difference. We could then say, for example, that an atom and a mountain were equal, since there would be no real difference in size between them.
From the claim that the chain of smaller parts must eventually come to an end, and that atoms can no longer be divided beyond that point, they concluded that atoms are not eternal.

Following this logic, the question of the creation of the world could be raised only together with the question of its disappearance, because if we accept disappearance, we must also accept coming into existence.
On this question of coming into existence and passing away, they reasoned as follows:
If atoms are infinite, there is no need to ask when they began.
But all ordinary things are temporary.
This means that they have both a beginning and an end.
If we now compare the atomism of Nyaya–Vaisheshika with that of the ancient Greek school, what do we find?
Let us look again at Chattopadhyaya, who states the issue very directly:
“Our view of the atomic theory of Nyaya–Vaisheshika must be connected with our view of its relationship to the corresponding theory in ancient Greece.

“In the history of ancient Greek philosophy, Democritus proposed the atomic hypothesis as a rational way of solving the problems of his age, especially problems that had already been raised by thinkers such as Parmenides and Heraclitus.”
“Parmenides, to some extent, has a parallel in the idealism of the Upanishads, since he recognized one reality: a single, unchanging being.
“Heraclitus, on the other hand, was in some respects like our early Buddhists. For him, the only reality was change, or becoming.”
We can understand Chattopadhyaya’s point in the following way.
In Greece, atomism first appeared as an attempt to solve the problems raised by two opposing views.
On one side stood Parmenides, who spoke of true being and denied change.
On the other stood Heraclitus, who recognized nothing except change.
The Upanishads insisted on a single, unchanging being.
Buddha, by contrast, recognized only change.
Buddha used the image of a candle flame to describe this constant change, just as Heraclitus used the image of flowing river water.
If this is what Chattopadhyaya means, then the comparison leads to a further conclusion.

Just as the ancient Greek atomists tried to find a way of reconciling the view of Parmenides with that of Heraclitus, the Indian atomists tried to find a way of reconciling the Upanishadic view with the early Buddhist view.
“It is not difficult to see the strong similarity with the situation faced by the followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika.
“On one side stood the teaching of the Upanishads, with its eternal and unchanging Brahman. On the other stood the Buddhist doctrine of a continuous stream—the stream of change.
“The followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika found a way out of this contradiction through atomic theory.
“They argued that eternal, unchanging atoms could explain being, while the different ways in which those atoms combine, separate, and recombine could explain becoming.
“But the Nyaya–Vaisheshika system lacked many important elements of Democritus’s theory, especially one of its central elements: the motion of atoms.”
Chattopadhyaya then comments on this last point:
“Nyaya atomism developed, to some extent, in the opposite direction.
“Kanada, one of the founders of the Nyaya school, did not even mention God. He was most likely an atheist.
“Later philosophers who followed this method, however, were not merely believers in God. They found themselves in the front ranks of those who offered proofs for his existence.
“Why did our atomism meet this particular fate?
